after.scope_note: Earlier roots and literary practices overlap with modern historical biography without forming one origin story. Plutarch is one ancient example; Johnson’s private lives precede Carlyle’s Heroes. Strachey names particular models and sources, and Woolf distinguishes his achievements and failures. Her English canon is not a universal history of biography. Translations and abridgments mediate the texts encountered here; named literary resources do not by themselves establish a school’s founding.

strands.title: Character and selective lives

strands.title: Private particulars, conversation and narrative

strands.title: Creative individuals and historical belief
strands.focus: Carlyle’s lecture opening connects great individuals with historical creation and religious conviction. It does not define all nineteenth-century life writing, or all his own writing.

strands.title: Compact portraits and acknowledged models
strands.focus: Strachey chooses concentrated portraits, invokes French eloges and uses Cook’s research. Selection is a stated artistic procedure, not representative sampling of the whole age.

strands.title: Checkable evidence and invention
strands.focus: Woolf’s contrasting judgments of Strachey’s royal biographies test how documentary limits constrain imaginative form. Her conclusions remain criticism, not a settled law of biography.

strands.title: Discontinuous narration and the coherent self
strands.focus: Levi and Bourdieu use named literary experiments to question retrospective coherence. The novels are resources for later arguments, not automatic origins of historical schools.

strands.title: Abridgment and later readers
strands.focus: Osgood explains what his Boswell selection removes. A widely accessible edition is a particular editorial construction of the work.

after.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

added.evidence_note: The complete 1989 essay accepts Bourdieu’s warning but emphasizes bounded room to act within contradictory norms. This methodological contribution coexists with the undirected comparison of biography and microhistory; it does not make all life writing microstoria.

added.relationship: Levi questions assumed group cohesion in Chartier’s account of representations and practices
added.evidence_note: Printed pp. 1334–1335 and notes 18/20 target the essay in La rappresentazione del sociale (1989). Levi values the intervention but argues that individuals and groups need distinct procedures and that group formation itself needs explanation. Do not conflate this citation with another 1989 French article or generalize to all Chartier.
added.map_label: Levi: how are coherent groups produced?

added.relationship: Robbe-Grillet’s challenge to coherent life narration supplies Bourdieu with an explicit literary resource
added.evidence_note: Bourdieu cites Le Miroir qui revient (1984), p. 208, while declining to adopt all the associated philosophy. The original literary work remains mediated; this is a specific resource for the 1986 essay, not the origin of all practice theory.

added.relationship: Levi uses discontinuous and dialogic literary narration to question the uniformly coherent historical actor
added.evidence_note: Sterne and Diderot are named examples in the 1989 essay. This is a documented later methodological use, not a claim that novels founded Italian microhistory; the original novels were not read here.
added.map_label: Levi’s literary examples and historical actors

added.relationship: Woolf tests the limits of Strachey’s literary biography through contrasting royal lives
added.evidence_note: Her 1939 essay praises Queen Victoria while criticizing Elizabeth and Essex for its combination of invention and limited evidence. Preserve the positive judgment and the specificity of her target; it is not a uniform condemnation of Strachey or literary form.

before.relationship: sustains narrative and life-centered forms of history
before.evidence_note: Long-lived narrative and biographical practices provide context; Carlyle and Strachey neither founded nor exhausted biography.

after.relationship: Compare inherited life-writing practices with modern historical uses of biography
after.evidence_note: Plutarch, Johnson, Carlyle, Strachey and Woolf pose distinct questions about character, selection and evidence. The teaching overlap remains undirected; neither Carlyle nor Strachey founded or exhausted biography.

before.relationship: overlaps in intensive life-based inquiry; aims differ
before.evidence_note: A close study of a life need not belong to Italian microstoria; methods and purposes must be compared.

after.relationship: Compare intensive life-based inquiry with microhistorical questions about scale and social relations
after.evidence_note: A close study of a life is not automatically Italian microstoria. Levi’s 1989 distinctions clarify differences between modal, contextual, extreme-case and dialogic uses, and make group formation and bounded agency questions for inquiry. This comparison remains undirected alongside his separately evidenced methodological contribution.
after.map_label: Life inquiry, scale and bounded agency

before.relationship: Women’s histories recover lives and revise biographical significance
before.evidence_note: Recovery of lives revises historical significance; life writing also has independent, much older roots. Davis’s Women on the Margins (1995) supplies a named three-life project, currently supported by catalogue description rather than a full source audit.

after.relationship: Davis’s comparative biographies develop through women’s-history teaching, source discovery and revised questions of significance
after.evidence_note: Davis names the 1971 course with Conway and Colie’s Glikl suggestion in her acknowledgments. Her prologue and conclusion compare three lives while retaining religious difference and colonial power. This primary selection supplements the existing catalogue description; it is not a full source audit or a claim that women’s history originated biography.
after.map_label: Davis, Conway and Colie: teaching into research

before.evidence_note: Cultural approaches examine how selves are made and represented; the claim concerns a methodological resource.

after.relationship: Davis examines stories, self-representation and culturally situated differences within comparative life history
after.evidence_note: The Glikl opening uses Certeau’s account of stories; prologue and conclusion test categories, religious commitments and power. This named case specifies a cultural resource without making every biography a cultural-history application or treating an imagined dialogue as testimony.

added.citation: Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841), Lecture I, 5 May 1840, opening selection.

verification.note: First seven lecture paragraphs completely read. Creative great individuals and practical religious belief structure the account; religious hierarchy and disparaging language remain situated judgments. Remaining lecture/book unread. Power’s earlier checked quotation from another Carlyle text does not license reducing all his work to this selection; its original remains uncollated.

added.citation: Lytton Strachey, Eminent Victorians (1918), preface and postscript.

verification.note: Complete preface and postscript read. Selection, French eloges models and an explicit debt to Edward Cook’s Nightingale biography support particular claims. Ranke/Gibbon are rhetorical comparisons, not documented personal critics. Incidental Manning opening is not a complete life; Strachey’s claim to impartiality is not an independent audit.

added.title: Virginia Woolf, “The Art of Biography,” The Atlantic, April 1939.
added.citation: Virginia Woolf, “The Art of Biography,” The Atlantic, April 1939.

verification.note: Complete sections I–IV read at https://www.literaturecambridge.co.uk/news/Woolf-biography; archive date and sections I–III subsequently checked here. Supports Woolf’s different judgments of Strachey’s Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, checkable evidence, selection and changing conventions. Her restricted English canon is not a universal history; her praise does not certify all Victoria facts. Cambridge footer’s collection date is unreliable. A Gutenberg Australia transcription repeats typos; Leonard Woolf’s complete editorial note describes posthumous mediation. Original print scan and section IV archive wording uncollated; The New Biography unread.

Bourdieu disagreement is explicitly one of emphasis; scientific absurdity refers to an individual/society opposition, not all biography. Roche, Venturi and literary works remain mediated. Notes 18/20 identify Chartier’s Italian collection essay, not automatically another French 1989 article.

verification.note: Public OCR read: title/edition; complete prologue pp. 1–4, conclusion pp. 203–216 and acknowledgments pp. 340–344; selected Glikl opening pp. 6–8 and conclusion notes 1–8/start of 9. Main chapters and remaining notes not fully read. Prologue is an imagined October 1994 dialogue. Certeau and Foucault are explicit resources; editions/translations and collaboration are discussed. Original manuscripts, Glikl editions and clinical work uncollated. Pappenheim was treated by Breuer, not Freud; Davis’s reconstruction of her likely feelings is conjectural. This primary selection supplements, rather than retroactively upgrades, the existing catalogue record.

lifetradition.people: Expand the two-person roster with Plutarch, English Samuel Johnson, James Boswell, Woolf, explicit models/resources Mason, Fontenelle, Condorcet and Cook, and literary examples Sterne, Diderot and Robbe-Grillet. Osgood represents editorial mediation. Keep English Johnson distinct from the existing Yoruba historian and James distinct from John Boswell. These are shared profiles, not new full graph entries or exclusive professional classifications.
lifetradition.works_and_arguments: Read Plutarch’s opening paragraph, complete Johnson Rambler 60, seven displayed Boswell opening paragraphs and Osgood’s complete preface, Carlyle’s first seven Lecture I paragraphs, complete Strachey preface/postscript and complete Woolf essay. Titles and original/reprint dates remain distinct. Literary works cited by Levi/Bourdieu and Strachey’s models remain mediated; no invented publication years are assigned to those unspecified here.
lifetradition.internal_distinctions: Seven approaches distinguish ancient character, private particulars/conversation, heroic belief, concentrated portraits, evidence/invention, discontinuous selves and abridgment. Johnson’s earlier interest in private lives and Woolf’s criteria prevent a linear great-men-to-ordinary-people origin story. Carlyle’s opening is not all his writing; Strachey’s portraits are deliberately selected, not representative sampling.
lifetradition.incoming_connections: Woolf’s specific criticism of Elizabeth and Essex supplies a new incoming critical exchange while retaining her praise of Victoria. Existing Power-to-Carlyle relation remains correctly oriented as a resource used by Power; the original Carlyle passage quoted there is not newly collated. Mason/Cook/French eloges are named within rosters and approaches rather than fabricated graph-person arrows.
lifetradition.outgoing_connections: Add Bourdieu’s explicit Robbe-Grillet resource and Levi’s named literary examples as contributions to particular later methodological arguments. Preserve edge_038 as an undirected comparison with biography and the earlier Power contribution. No claim that the cited novels founded microhistory or that one literary tradition originated all practice theory.
lifetradition.evidence_and_interpretation: Primary passages, authorial accuracy claims, editorial abridgment and mediated citations are distinguished. Woolf’s limited English canon and Carlyle’s religious hierarchy are situated positions. Atlantic archive confirms April 1939 and sections I–III; full I–IV reading uses the Cambridge transcription, whose collection-date footer is not adopted. Original editions and non-European breadth remain bounded questions.

biography.people: Preserve seventeen prior identities and original representative prose; expand with earlier biographers, Woolf, Bourdieu, Levi, Roche/Venturi, Glikl editors/translators and named Davis collaborators. Pappenheim appears as translator, not only as Anna O. Existing labour, Black, social, political and narrative lives retain their particular contributions and critics. No individual profile is claimed as a full-node review.
biography.works_and_arguments: Davis’s full prologue, conclusion and acknowledgments plus selected Glikl opening support comparative method and fill her neighboring cultural-history work blank. Bourdieu’s full four-page essay and Levi’s complete twelve pages provide primary methodological arguments. Glikl editions, Roche/Venturi and novels remain mediated. Erikson’s Luther remains metadata-supported and Freud’s blank remains pending for the next substantive batch, rather than filled from a passing clinical reference.
biography.internal_distinctions: Add eight approaches to the four preserved approaches: selection/significance, relational trajectories, scale/agency, contextual reconstruction, comparative margins, translation of records, teaching/collaboration and psychoanalytic lives. Davis’s explicitly imagined dialogue tests categories without becoming testimony. Neither a universal female experience nor a linear history of progress is inferred from the comparative ordering.
biography.incoming_connections: Specify women’s-history teaching through Conway, Colie and Davis, and cultural stories through Davis’s actual passages. Add Certeau’s explicit resource, Foucault’s cited power argument, Bourdieu’s criticism and Levi’s methodological contribution. Retain existing contributions by Brown, Torr, Power, Cam, Wedgwood and Tuchman, and the separate metadata-scoped Erikson link; shared vocabulary alone creates no additional influence arrows.
biography.outgoing_connections: Add Levi’s particular criticism of Chartier’s group formation assumptions and Woolf’s contrasting judgment of Strachey’s royal lives. Preserve comparisons with political history and microhistory as undirected; Levi’s contribution coexists without reclassification. Delbrück’s biographical trajectory and earlier biographical criticisms remain intact. No generic reciprocal cultural-history edge is added simply because Davis belongs to both contexts.
biography.evidence_and_interpretation: Bourdieu criticizes constructed coherence without rejecting all agency; Levi explicitly presents a different but not contradictory emphasis. Levi’s Chartier target is the Italian collection essay in notes 18/20, not automatically another French 1989 article. Davis’s interpretations of manuscripts, colonial relationships and likely feelings remain attributed. Breuer treated Pappenheim; Freud’s coauthorship is not therapy. OCR, edition, translation and reading limits are explicit.

lifetradition: Examine a bounded scholarly introduction and one translated entry from Ibn Khallikan’s Wafayat al-ayan, using a pre-2000 edition where available, to test the current selection’s European/Anglophone weighting. Document the text’s own purposes, selection and transmission; do not infer a generic Islamic-to-European biography genealogy.

Collate one of the seven currently read Boswell opening paragraphs and one omitted adjacent methodological passage against a complete original or scholarly edition. Compare with Osgood’s stated omissions; resolve precisely what the accessible 1917 selection conceals without claiming a whole-book collation.
biography: Compare one short Glikl story or moral reflection in Pappenheim’s 1910 and Feilchenfeld’s 1913 translations, or document concrete witness/access limits. Davis’s conclusion supplies the specific critical claim but is not an independent edition collation; do not turn her conjecture about Pappenheim’s feelings into fact.

Read a bounded primary methodological passage from Erikson’s Young Man Luther (1958) during the next psychoanalysis/psychohistory batch, plus a specific critical reception if available. The present attribution is metadata-only, and Levi’s generic dismissal must not stand in for an Erikson-specific argument.
